Load shedding Funerals

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The impact of load shedding on load shedding is crippling South African undertakers. What will ease the pressure on the already struggling industry?

Unique Selling Point:
Continuous load shedding is increasingly becoming funeral homes with some having to close their doors and others battling to keep mortuary fridges cold because of the high additional cost of running generators. Scrambling for solutions, families are being urged to bury their families in less than three days. Is the call feasible in a country with complex beliefs and practices.

Summary:
Running a funeral business is not easy. It is an important and expensive act of service. We hear from funeral parlours how much much electricity it takes to run mortuaries - from customers to the owners of the businesses. We explore the emotional layers of honouring the dead and how the call by associations could prevent some South African families from doing that.

Press Release:


The Business of Burials

Running a funeral business is never easy. It’s an important service, helping clients give their loved ones a dignified send-off. But before the deceased can be buried with dignity, they should be stored with dignity as well. But South Africa’s energy crisis is threatening this to0. Around the country, power cuts have had a dire impact on the funeral homes, with some having to close their doors and others battling to keep mortuary fridges cold because of the high additional cost of running generators. Scrambling for solutions, families are being urged to bury their families within three days. But in a country where it often takes a week or two weeks for some cultural burial rites to be performed, is this the best solution? Carte Blanche investigates.

Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:



INTRO: Rolling electricity blackouts… disruptive… crippling for the economy… and for a man from Johannesburg, a horror story …with unexpected twists… and terrible consequences.

EST TUMELO

Tumelo Boleme knew that his elderly grandmother in the Free State was quite ill. That she was admitted to hospital.


What he didn’t know.. until only two days later.. was that she’d passed away.

It was LAST April…the year in which Eskom implemented over two hundred days of loadshedding.


TUMELO BOLEME
(((lets include claire's question about what happened ))
00:51 – 01:13 She passed away on the Tuesday, but I received the message on Thursday.
01:14 – 01:20 So that’s why they couldn’t get hold of me.
10:49 – I still blame load shedding for my grandmother’s death. Because the hospital in Thaba-Nchu, doesn’t have a backup generator.
CLAIRE – What?!
11:09 - I’m telling you...


VO – The hospital had no generator to keep the lights on.. Tumelo was in shock…but loadshedding wasn’t done with him.
His grandmother’s body was taken to a local funeral parlour where she’d stay… until the Boleme family could assemble back home for her funeral…
BREATHE
But like for a growing number of death-care providers, their undertaker battled to keep her body COLD enough for LONG enough.


TUMELO BOLEME
03:28 – 03:36 - At the time of the funeral the body left the hospital and it was taken to the funeral parlor. As a result of load shedding the body could not be preserved properly.




VO - During the night, hours before taking it home, body fluid STARTED dripping from his grandmother’s casket…


TUMELO BOLEME
06:22 – 06:31 Friday at the mortuary water was already dripping from the casket.
06:32 – 06:48 - We got home with a leaking body. The whole night water was just dripping from the casket like (makes dripping sound)


VO – With his grandmother’s remains decomposing after a week…the undertaker warned the family not to hold the casket by the handles.. eaten away by body fluids…and definitely NOT …to view the body.


TUMELO BOLEME
07:22 – 07:28 I couldn’t give my grandmother a decent, dignified burial because of everything that was happening.


VO - This year.. Eskom has implemented loadshedding every day so far .. And for many undertakers it’s become an ordeal JUST to keep giving their customers what they need.
BREATHE


LINK - Death is big business in South Africa… the funeral services industry generates revenue of more than R7,5 billion each year. It is a thriving…and highly competitive industry. But load shedding is putting a spanner in the works, especially for smaller funeral businesses that have to fork out growing amounts of cash to keep generators running.


VO - It’s 9am on a Monday at Konyana funerals in Johannesburg. Apart from business running a little slow, the lights are on.
Lawrence Konyana took over a thriving family business that was founded in the sixties…but these days he feels like he’s feeding all his profits into a generator.


LAWRENCE KONYANA – KONYANA FUNERALS
08:27 – 08:35 - You've got to make sure that the integrity of that body is kept, because if the fridge is not working, that means it's going to decompose.
08:44 – 08:49 - So it's very much important that we make sure that we always have constant power.


VO – Operational costs have always been high, but the Covid pandemic hit Lawrence hard… contrary to what people might imagine, it wasn’t just a case of more deaths.. more funerals.. and more profits…


LAWRENCE KONYANA – KONYANA FUNERALS
02:49 - ... you had one or two or three members of the same family dying within a week or within a few days of each other. And they probably buried the first one decently. The second one and the third one there's no funds and they will still come to you. And what do you do?


VO – In a local deathcare market of about 70,000 small operators, only 10,000 legal undertakers generate most of the profits…
Now add in a pandemic …and loadshedding, that’s seen generators –meant for backup– becoming the main power source… it put the very viability of small businesses at risk.


LAWRENCE KONYANA – KONYANA FUNERALS
05:55 – 06:07 - ...we normally get 2000 litres of diesel. And that will last us just around a month or six weeks, if we are lucky.
06:08 – 06:20 - And we used to spend just under 30 grand for that. ... And now we're spending almost double.


LINK - The law says funeral parlors must have a backup system…a generator on-site… to keep the storage rooms cool in the event of load-shedding. But with the rapidly rising cost of fuel …how long can it remain sustainable?


VO: Dududu Magano is spokesperson for the National Funeral Directors’ Association.


DUDUDU MAGANO – NATIONAL FUNERAL DIRECTORS' ASSOCIATION
09:21 – 09:33 - A disaster would be an understatement.
06:38 – 06:47 - A 30 minutes notice, we are on stage five. 30 minutes notice, we are on stage six; and that meant that you are going without power for a number of hours. It put a strain on income.
VO – Ironically, while operators fork out more of their own cash to keep going, families are opting for smaller burial packages.


VO – It’s strangling even older and bigger franchises, with much deeper pockets.
Doves Head office supports independent franchises country-wide. CEO Jodene Smith.


JODENE SMITH – DOVES CEO
We found that our businesses started shutting down. We had an effect on our phone lines.
01:14 – 01:28 - People couldn't call us. We had an increase break-ins…the branches were vulnerable.


VO – Then, with generators running virtually all day, the cost of the diesel started spiraling. Last year, the company invested in a backup solution for all its branches.




JODENE SMITH – DOVES CEO
04:55 – 05:05 That cost us up to 1.7 million. We have 128 branches across country. So it was a massive impact on us.


DEATH CARE SEQUENCE
VO – For many undertakers it’s a matter of pride to prepare the deceased for burial.
BREATH
…an important moment for grieving families….
But to manage costs, some are now asking families to bury their loved ones more quickly… at least within four days.
That would never have worked for Tumelo’s family.
Loadshedding disabled every institution he depended on to expedite a funeral.


TUMELO BOLEME
02:10 – 02:28 - The first thing I needed to do was to get leave from work because there had been a death in the family. They wanted a death certificate as proof and they couldn’t get it that side because of load shedding at Home Affairs.
03:02 – 03:11 - I then went to the insurance company to put in a claim, I couldn’t claim without a death certificate.


VO – Without a death certificate to submit for an insurance claim the family had to scrape together their savings to conduct the funeral.
Tumelo would only get the death certificate the week AFTER her burial…and by then, he was facing a disciplinary at work…for leaving without submitting it.


TUMELO BOLEME
18:21 – 18:30 - When a person dies, we believe in ancestors. We religiously go to the cemetery. But how can I go to my grandmothers grave knowing that I wronged her?


CLAIRES BEAUTIFUL REFLECTIVE LINK

“Even if…that i never anticipated”


VO – The days following death are sacred.. punctuated by rituals that give the bereaved closure …and pave the way into the afterlife for the deceased.
Dr Zulumathabo Zulu studies the significance of these practices.
DR ZULUMATHABO ZULU CULTURAL EXPERT
03:19 – 03:28 - Preservation of the body, integrity of the body, is extremely important, which is why you have these cleansing rituals.
01:43 – 01:55 - Where, for example, the body will be cleansed using special medicine plants.
01:56 – 02:08 - And the idea here is that in addition to the actual cleansing, is to empower the spirit of the deceased.


Since the ramifications of not giving the deceased a dignified send-off can be dire, some who can afford it…go for embalming - a chemical treatment THAT DELAYS decomposition and costs between 1 500 and 3 000 Rand.


DR ZULUMATHABO ZULU CULTURAL EXPERTS
20:19 – 20:31 - other African countries like Kenya, they provide embalming services. People embalm the body and apparently the government pays for it.
23:30 – 23:45 - ... I think the government can play a big role in terms of helping to solve this issue. So that it’s not just the burden that is carried by the funeral parlour.


VO – To combat outages, the government this week announced a tax incentives for solar roof panels.. businesses will be able to claim up to R15 000.
But Dududu Magano and Lawrence Konyana SAY that after investing so heavily in generators, the cost of solar - even subsidized….is way too high.
And it’s too late FOR MANY like Tumelo…haunted by the memory of his grandmother's shambles of a funeral.


TUMELO BOLEME
08:00 – 08:06 - I feel like I failed her, I don’t want to lie to you.
08:08 – 08:15 - Sometimes things aren’t going well for me. I’m a black person who does rituals. Sometimes I feel like she’s turned her back on me.
18:39 – It’s killing me inside.
